challenges.argument: Option [1] is a concrete scene and partially matches later details: the volunteer crew would handle 'litter pickup, mulching, and repainting the picnic shelters,' so peeling shelters and litter are plausibly consistent. However, 'sits nearly empty' contradicts the survey of 212 people 'outside the park gate on two Saturdays' and the bakery owner's claim that 'weekend park traffic brings in roughly a third of her sales.' It also shows a neglected park rather than what free access puts at stake. Key [2] is clearly better.

Option [3] does make a debatable claim ('charging students to use a park they already help maintain is unfair') and gestures at the volunteer labor in paragraph 3, but it does not preview the revenue argument of paragraph 2 ('the fee would raise less money than it appears to'). Key [0] previews both in order. Minor quibble: 'at no cost to the town' slightly overstates since the crew is 'supervised by parks staff,' but this doesn't undermine the key.

Option [1] accurately restates the data ('nearly two thirds... almost a third') but merely paraphrases sentence 7 without explaining the link to the revenue claim in sentence 5 ('the fee would raise less money than it appears to'). Key [3] supplies the missing inference about fees collected from a smaller crowd.

Placing sentence 9 after sentence 7 would let 'but that figure assumes attendance stays flat' function as a rebuttal immediately following the survey evidence, and would keep sentence 8's bakery detail as a separate extension. But the stem explicitly asks for movement 'from the commission's revenue assumption to the evidence that challenges it,' which requires the assumption to precede sentences 6–7. Key [0] is correct.

Option [3] 'a clear case of fiscal negligence' is confident and budget-minded, but 'negligence' accuses the commission of dereliction, which is not 'a respectful tone appropriate for the commission.' Option [0] keeps confidence ('costly') while remaining courteous. Key is sound.

Option [0] ('every member plans to major in engineering and will credit the school for that choice') at least gestures at an institutional outcome a board might value (student futures, school reputation), so a reader might see it as an appeal to board values. But it is wholly unsupported by the passage and overclaims ('every member'), so it is clearly inferior to the key. The real problem is with the key's own factual grounding: it says the team 'kept eleven students meeting every week for eight months,' yet sentence 12 says 'attendance never dropped below nine members,' which means not all eleven met every week, and the passage never states that meetings were weekly. The key is still the best option, but its claim slightly overstates what the passage supports—ironically the very fault the passage's sentence 14 is being revised to fix.
challenges.key_flaw: Justification says 'both details are supported by sentences 1 and 12,' but sentence 12 supports only that attendance 'never dropped below nine,' not that 'eleven students' met 'every week'; the passage never specifies weekly meetings. Also 'nothing but donated and secondhand equipment' describes the August starting inventory (sentence 1), not necessarily the entire season.

challenges.argument: Option [0] ('members gave up many Saturdays to keep working on Marmalade') is specific-sounding and concrete, and a careless reader might take sustained effort as evidence of learning. However, it documents time spent, not skills gained, so it does not support the claim in sentence 10 that members 'learned a great deal.' The key's before-and-after ('could not define a gear ratio in September wrote the technical notebook that the judges scored in April') is clearly superior.

Option [3] ('Robots, like people, have good days and bad days') is the only other option that offers a genuinely accessible comparison for non-engineers and ties back to the November drive-base problem. But it attributes the failure to luck rather than a diagnosable cause, which undercuts rather than advances 'the argument that the team learned to solve problems efficiently.' Option [1] contains a comparison but says the opposite of the intended point; option [0] has no comparison at all. The key is clearly best.

Option [0] ('The adjudicating personnel expressed considerable astonishment regarding the operational status of our apparatus') is unquestionably formal, and a reader focused only on the word 'formal' might choose it. But its inflated diction is stilted rather than appropriately formal, and 'considerable astonishment' still overstates the reaction, failing the 'without overstating' criterion. Option [3] overstates ('Every judge... most impressive'); [2] keeps the casual tone. The key's measured attribution to 'Two of the judges' is best, though note it introduces a detail (the judges speaking to the adviser) not in the passage, which the stem implicitly permits.

No alternative is defensible. [0] is a comma splice with 'however' used as a conjunctive adverb between commas; [1] moves 'by March' to the first clause, changing the meaning (that students had never used a drill before March) and still leaves a comma splice; [3] remains a comma splice ('before, by March, they were teaching') and adds an unnecessary comma before 'who visited.' The semicolon in [2] is the only correct join that preserves meaning.

A reader could argue that the nine-year tally of 'roughly four thousand bug reports' builds the writer's ethos as a veteran maintainer, and ¶1 explicitly frames her experience ('I spent nine years maintaining a small text-parsing library') as the lens for reading Alcock. But the option misfires on its object: she never challenges 'the findings of Alcock's survey'; she calls the diagnosis 'a good one' and reserves her challenge for the cure. The paragraph's rhetorical question ('Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them') and the closing 'several thousand of us who were standing on her work' aim squarely at the reader's complicity, supporting the key.

The sentence ends 'and Alcock tells that story well,' which a partial reader could take as praise for the second half's writing. But the review's quality judgment is about argument, not prose ('the book loses its footing'), and the sentence's structural role is unmistakably the concession set up by 'I will grant that money has saved projects' and closed by 'But a stipend changes what the work is.' The key is sound.

The clause continues 'the smallest libraries will still rely on the stubbornness of individuals,' which a careless reader might read as returning responsibility to individual maintainers. However, this is an acknowledged residue, not a shift in the proposal: the sentence's main clause affirms that the plan 'would spread the weight across the walls that bear it,' i.e., onto dependent institutions. Option [1] is clearly wrong because the text says individuals' stubbornness, not 'corporate sponsorship.' The key's reading as scope-limiting concession fits the semicolon structure.
challenges.stem_issue: The stem presupposes the acknowledgment 'strengthens' the argument; acceptable for AP conventions but slightly leading.

challenges.argument: ¶2 does describe a problem ('load-bearing walls that no inspector has visited'), and ¶3 is about remedy, so a skimming reader might select [1]. But ¶3 presents Alcock's cure ('His remedy is sponsorship'), which the writer rejects; her own solution ('The better cure') does not appear until ¶5. The key's quotations are accurate.

The sentence does set up the pivot to ¶5's alternative cure, and the key's own justification concedes it is 'preparing the alternative cure in paragraph 5.' A reader could thus say it 'introduces' the proposal. But the sentence itself mentions nothing about engineers' hours; the proposal is introduced by 'The better cure is already visible in the margins of his own book.' The sentence's primary work is the pivot from anecdote back to Alcock ('Alcock understands this loneliness') and the critique of 'his faith in a check,' as the key says. [2] fails because 'puzzling' sharpens rather than softens criticism.

No alternative has real footing. [0] misreads the target: the hospital network is the one correspondent who said 'thank you,' so anger at it is unsupported. [1] contradicts 'companies I was never allowed to name' (plural users). [3] is undercut by 'roughly four thousand,' which signals estimate rather than precise records. The key's description of brevity and understatement matches the text.
